title: \bf Definition
body_md:
Assume $S$ is real-analytic near the origin. Let $S(x,y) =\sum_{\alpha,\beta \ge 0} c_{\alpha,\beta} x^\alpha y^\beta$ be the Taylor expansion of $S$. Then the reduced Newton polyhedron $N(S)$ is the convex hull of
$$\bigcup_{\alpha,\beta\in \mathbb{N}^{\ast}}\{(x,y):x\geq \alpha,~y\geq\beta\},$$
 where the union is taken over all positive integers $\alpha,\beta$ such that $c_{\alpha,\beta}\neq 0$.

label: Lemma operator vers van der Corput
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lemma operator vers van der Corput}
Let $T_\lambda$ be defined as {\rm (\ref{Def-T-lambda-Section1})} with the cut-off $\varphi$ supported in a curved trapezoid $\Omega$, where $\Omega$ is contained in a sufficiently small neighborhood of the origin. Assume the phase $S(x,y)$ is a real-valued real-analytic function near the origin. If the following assumptions are true:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[{\rm (i)}] For some $\mu, A>0$, the Hessian $S_{xy}''$ satisfies
$\mu\leq\left|S_{xy}''(x,y)\right|\leq A\mu$ for $(x,y)\in \Omega;$
\item[{\rm (ii)}] Let $\delta_{\Omega,h}(x)$ be the length of the vertical cross section of $\Omega$ at $x$. For some $M>0$,
\[
\sum_{k=0}^2\sup_{\Omega}\left(\delta_{\Omega,h}(x)\right)^k
|\partial_y^k\varphi(x,y)|\leq M,
\]
\end{enumerate}
\noindent then there exists a constant $C$, independent of $\mu$ and $M$, such that for all $g\in L^2(\Bbb R)$
\[
\|T_\lambda g\|_{L^2}\leq CM(|\lambda|\mu)^{-1/2}\|g\|_{L^2}.
\]

label: Lemma-upper-Lp-bound
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By integration by parts, it is easy to see that
\begin{eqnarray*}
R_jf(t,x)
&=&
\Phi\left( \frac{x}{2^j} \right)
\int_{\Bbb R}\eta(t+x^my,y) e^{izy} dy \\
&=&
\Phi\left( \frac{x}{2^j} \right)
\left( \frac{1}{iz} \right)^N
\int_{\Bbb R}\eta(t+x^my,y) \frac{d^N}{dy^N}\Big(e^{izy} \Big) dy\\
&=&
\Phi\left( \frac{x}{2^j} \right)
\left(- \frac{1}{iz} \right)^N
\int_{\Bbb R}\frac{d^N}{dy^N}\Big(\eta(t+x^my,y) \Big) e^{izy} dy.
\end{eqnarray*}
Observe that
\begin{eqnarray*}
\frac{d^N}{dy^N}\Big(\eta(t+x^my,y) \Big)
&=&
\Big\{\Big((x^m,1)\cdot \nabla\Big)^N\eta\Big\}
(t+x^my,y)\\
&=&
\sum_{k=0}^N C_N^k x^{m(N-k)}\partial_1^{N-k}
\partial_2^k\eta(t+x^my,y),
\end{eqnarray*}
where $\nabla=(\partial_1,\partial_2)$ is the gradient operator in the plane. For fixed $t$ and $x\approx 2^j$, it follows from $\eta\in C_0^{\infty}(\Bbb R^2)$ that $\{y:\eta(t+x^my,y)\neq 0\}$ is contained in an interval with length less than a constant multiple of $2^{-mj}$.
This implies, for positive $j$,
$$
|R_jf(t,x)|
\lesssim
\left(\frac{2^{mj}}{z}\right)^N 2^{-mj}.
$$
Similarly, if $R_jf(t,x)\neq 0$, then it is necessarily that $|t|\lesssim 2^{mj}$ and $x\approx 2^j$. Hence for any $p\geq 1$, we obtain
\begin{equation*}
\|R_jf\|_{L^p}
\lesssim
\left(\frac{2^{mj}}{z}\right)^N 2^{-mj}
2^{(m+1)j/p}.
\end{equation*}
The proof of the lemma is complete.
head: environment

label: Lemma-comparable-Lp-lemma
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: {\bf Remark}
body_md: This estimate is also true for larger $N$ provided that $j\geq j(m,N)$, where $j(m, N)$ is a sufficiently large number depending on $m$ and $N$. For our purpose, the estimates for $N=0,1,2$ are enough.

label: low-bound-Rjf
title: Proof
body_md:
For clarity, let $\epsilon_0=2^{-m-1}$. For $2^{\frac14} 2^{mj}+1\leq -t \leq 2^{\frac34} 2^{mj}-1$ and $2^{j-\frac1{4m}}\leq x \leq 2^{j+\frac1{4m}}$, the following estimate is true:
\begin{equation*}
\frac{-t-1}{x^m}\geq \frac{2^{\frac14} 2^{mj}}{2^{mj+\frac14}}=1,~~~
\frac{-t+1}{x^m}\leq \frac{2^{\frac34} 2^{mj}}{2^{mj-\frac14}}=2.
\end{equation*}
Observe that $\eta(X)=1$ for $X\in [-1,1]\times [1,2]$.
We claim that there exists a constant $C>0$, independent of $j$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{low-bound-Rjf}
|R_jf(t,x)|
\geq
C 2^{-mj}.
\end{equation}
In view of $\,{\rm supp}\,(f)\subseteq [-2,2]\times [\frac12,4]$, if $R_jf(t,x)\neq 0$ then $|t+x^my|\leq 2$. Hence, for $2^{j-1}\leq x \leq 2^{j+1}$,
$$
\left|y+\frac{t}{x^m} \right|
\leq
\frac{2}{x^m}
\leq
2^{-m(j-1)+1}.
$$
The oscillation term $e^{izy}$ can be removed essentially in $R_jf(t,x)$ for $t,x$ described as above. In fact, for $t\approx \epsilon_0 2^{mj}$ and $x\approx 2^j$, one sees that
\begin{equation*}
|R_jf(t,x)|
=
\left|
\Phi\left( \frac{x}{2^j} \right)
\int_{\Bbb R}\eta(t+x^my,y) e^{i\epsilon_0 2^{mj} (y+t/x^m)} dy
\right|
\geq
C
\Phi\left( \frac{x}{2^j} \right)
\int_{\Bbb R}\eta(t+x^my,y) dy,
\end{equation*}
where we have used the fact $\epsilon_0 2^{mj} |y+t/x^m|\leq 1$, and $\Phi,\eta$ are nonnegative functions. For those $y$ satisfying $|t+x^my|\leq 1$ and $1\leq y \leq 2$, our assumption on $\eta$ implies $\eta(t+x^my,y)=1$. Observe that
\begin{equation*}
|t+x^my|\leq 1
\Leftrightarrow
\frac{-1-t}{x^m}
\leq
y
\leq
\frac{1-t}{x^m}
\Rightarrow
1\leq y \leq 2
\end{equation*}
for $t,x$ described as above, i.e., $2^{\frac14} 2^{mj}+1\leq -t \leq 2^{\frac34} 2^{mj}-1$ and $2^{j-\frac1{4m}}\leq x \leq 2^{j+\frac1{4m}}$. This implies $|R_jf(t,x)|\geq C2^{-mj}$. Hence (\ref{comparable-Lp-norm}) is true for $N=0$.
\vspace{0.5 \baselineskip}

For positive integers $N$,
\begin{eqnarray*}
&&
\partial_1^N\eta(t+x^my,y)\\
&=&
x^{-Nm}
\left(
\Big((x^m,1)\cdot \nabla \Big)^N\eta
\right)
(t+x^my,y)
-
\sum_{k=1}^N C_N^k x^{-mk}\partial_1^{N-k}\partial_2^k
\eta(t+x^my,y),
\end{eqnarray*}
where $\partial_k\eta(x_1,x_2)=\partial_{x_k}\eta(x_1,x_2)$
for $k=1,2$. It follows that
\begin{eqnarray*}
\partial_t^NR_jf(t,x)
&=&
\Phi\left( \frac{x}{2^j} \right)
\partial_t^N
\int_{\Bbb R}\eta(t+x^my,y) e^{izy} dy\\
&=&
\Phi\left( \frac{x}{2^j} \right)
x^{-Nm}
\int_{\Bbb R}\left(
\Big((x^m,1)\cdot \nabla \Big)^N\eta
\right)
(t+x^my,y)e^{izy} dy\\
&&
-
\Phi\left( \frac{x}{2^j} \right)\sum_{k=1}^N C_N^k x^{-mk}\int_{\Bbb R}\partial_1^{N-k}\partial_2^k
\eta(t+x^my,y)e^{izy} dy\\
&=&
\Phi\left( \frac{x}{2^j} \right)
\left(
\frac{-iz}{x^m}
\right)^N
\int_{\Bbb R}
\eta(t+x^my,y)e^{izy} dy\\
&&
-
\Phi\left( \frac{x}{2^j} \right)\sum_{k=1}^N C_N^k x^{-mk}\int_{\Bbb R}\partial_1^{N-k}\partial_2^k
\eta(t+x^my,y)e^{izy} dy\\
&:=&
I_1-I_2.
\end{eqnarray*}
The result for $N=0$ implies that $\|I_1\|_{L^p}\approx 2^{-mj}2^{(m+1)j/p}$. By Lemma \ref{Lemma-upper-Lp-bound}, with $\eta$ replaced by $\partial_1^{N-k}\partial_2^k
\eta$, we obtain the upper estimate $$\|I_2\|_{L^p}\lesssim \sum_{k=1}^{N} C_N^k 2^{-mkj}
2^{-mj}2^{(m+1)j/p}\lesssim 2^{-2mj}2^{(m+1)j/p}.$$ Hence, for sufficiently large $j$, the estimate (\ref{comparable-Lp-norm}) is true.

label: L^p-estimate-dyadic-intervals
title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{Lemma-comparable-Lp-lemma}, we get $
\|\partial_t^{l}Rf \|_{\frac{m+1}{m}  }\geq \|\partial_t^{l}R_jf \|_{ \frac{m+1}{m}}\geq C>0 $ for $l=1,2,3,4,$ where $C$ is independent of $j$. For $k\in \mathbb{Z}$, nonnegative integers $a,b$, and $|x|\approx 2^k$,
\begin{equation*}
\left|
\int_{\Bbb R}\partial_1^a\partial_2^b\eta(t+x^my,y)e^{izy}dy
\right|
\lesssim
2^{-mk}.
\end{equation*}
Also, if the above integral does not vanish, then $|t|\lesssim 2^{mk}$. Hence the following $L^p$ bound
\begin{equation}\label{L^p-estimate-dyadic-intervals}
\left\|
\int_{\Bbb R}\partial_1^a\partial_2^b\eta(t+x^my,y)e^{izy}dy
\right\|_{ L_{t,x}^{ (m+1)/m }(|x|\approx 2^k)}
\lesssim
1
\end{equation}
is true with the implicit upper bound independent of $k$.


Now we turn to the proof of (\ref{Lemma-Lp-outside-annulus}). For any $M\geq 1$, we use the stationary phase method to obtain, for $|x|\leq 2^{j-M}$,
\begin{eqnarray*}
\partial_t^{l}Rf(t,x)
&=&
\int_{\Bbb R}\partial_t^{l}\eta(t+x^my,y)e^{izy}dy\\
&=&
\left( \frac{1}{iz} \right)^N
\int_{\Bbb R}\partial_t^{l}\eta(t+x^my,y) \frac{d^N}{dy^N}\Big(e^{izy} \Big) dy\\
&=&
\left(- \frac{1}{iz} \right)^N
\int_{\Bbb R}\frac{d^N}{dy^N}\Big(\partial_t^{l}\eta(t+x^my,y) \Big) e^{izy} dy\\
&=&
\left(- \frac{1}{iz} \right)^N
\int_{\Bbb R}
\sum_{k=0}^NC_N^kx^{m(N-k)}\partial_1^{N-k}\partial_2^k
\partial_t^{l}\eta(t+x^my,y)  e^{izy} dy.
\end{eqnarray*}
Here $\partial_1=\partial_t$. On the one hand, $\|\partial_t^{l}Rf\|_{L^{\frac{m+1}m}(|x|\leq 1)  }\lesssim 2^{-mNj}$ is obvious. On the other hand, for $|x|\approx 2^k$, $0\leq k\leq j-M$, we use the above estimates to obtain
\begin{equation*}
 \|\partial_t^{l}Rf\|_{L^{\frac{m+1}m}(|x|\approx 2^k)  }\lesssim 2^{mN(k-j)}
 \end{equation*}
By the triangle inequality on $L^p$, we get
\begin{equation*}
\|\partial_t^{l}Rf\|_{L^{\frac{m+1}m}(t\in\Bbb R,~|x|\leq 2^{j-M})  }\lesssim 2^{-mMN}.
\end{equation*}
It should be pointed out that this estimate is also true for $l=0$.

For positive integers $l$, we shall follow the argument in the proof of Lemma \ref{Lemma-comparable-Lp-lemma}. For $|x|\approx 2^k$, $k\geq j+M$, there holds
\begin{eqnarray*}
\partial_t^lRf(t,x)
&=&
\partial_t^l
\int_{\Bbb R}\eta(t+x^my,y) e^{izy} dy\\
&=&
x^{-ml}
\int_{\Bbb R}\left(
\Big((x^m,1)\cdot \nabla \Big)^l\eta
\right)
(t+x^my,y)e^{izy} dy\\
&&
-
\sum_{r=1}^l C_l^r x^{-mr}\int_{\Bbb R}\partial_1^{l-r}\partial_2^r
\eta(t+x^my,y)e^{izy} dy\\
&=&
\left(
\frac{-iz}{x^m}
\right)^l
\int_{\Bbb R}
\eta(t+x^my,y)e^{izy} dy\\
&&
-
\sum_{r=1}^l C_l^r x^{-mr}\int_{\Bbb R}\partial_1^{l-r}\partial_2^r
\eta(t+x^my,y)e^{izy} dy.
\end{eqnarray*}
Hence, by (\ref{L^p-estimate-dyadic-intervals}),
\begin{equation*}
 \|\partial_t^{l}Rf\|_{L^{\frac{m+1}m}(|x|\approx 2^k)  }\lesssim 2^{m(j-k)l}+2^{-mk},~~~l=1,2,3,4.
\end{equation*}
By the triangle inequality, we obtain
\begin{equation*}
 \|\partial_t^{l}Rf\|_{L^{\frac{m+1}m}(|x|\geq 2^{j+M})  }\lesssim 2^{-mMl}+2^{-mj-mM}
\end{equation*}
for positive integers $l$, and the implicit constant is independent of $j,M$. The proof of the lemma is complete.

title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
Let $n\geq 3$ be an integer. Assume $S(x,y)=\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_kx^{n-k}y^k$
with real coefficients $a_k$ and $a_1a_{n-1}\neq 0$.
If $Rf$ is defined by (\ref{Radon-transform}) with $\varphi(0,0,0)\neq0$, then there is no constant $C>0$ such that, for
all $f\in C_0^{\infty}(\Bbb R^2)$,
\begin{equation*}
\left\|
|\partial_t|^{\frac1n} Rf
\right\|_{L^p(\Bbb R^2)}
\leq
 C\|f\|_{L^p(\Bbb R^2)},~~~p\in \left\{\frac{n}{n-1},n\right\}.
\end{equation*}
head: environment

title: {\bf Remark}
body_md: The above inequality is true for $\frac{n}{n-1}<p<n$. This can be proved by an analytic interpolation argument; see Phong and Stein \cite{PS1994}. Hence the endpoint Sobolev regularity is not true. This contrasts the endpoint $L^p$ estimates for oscillatory integral operators with homogeneous polynomial phases $S(x,y)$; see Shi-Yan \cite{ShiYan}.

title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
Assume $S(x,y)$ is a real analytic function near the origin. Let $N(S''_{xy})$ be the Newton polyhedron of $S''_{xy}$. Denote by $(A_L,B_L)$ and $(A_R,B_R)$ the leftmost and rightmost extreme points of $N(S''_{xy})$, respectively. Then we have the following results:\\

\noindent {\rm(i)} If $A_L>B_L$ and $\varphi(0,0,0)\neq 0$, then there is no constant $C>0$ such that for all
$f\in C_0^{\infty}$
\begin{equation*}
\left\|
|\partial_t|^{\delta}Rf
\right\|_{L^p}
\leq
C\|f\|_{L^p},~~~\frac{A_L+B_L+2}{A_L+1}\leq p <2,
\end{equation*}
where $\delta=\frac{1}{A_L+1}\cdot\frac{1}{p}$.\\

\noindent {\rm(ii)} If $A_R<B_R$ and $\varphi(0,0,0)\neq 0$, then there is no constant $C>0$ such that for all
$f\in C_0^{\infty}$
\begin{equation*}
\left\|
|\partial_t|^{\delta}Rf
\right\|_{L^p}
\leq
C\|f\|_{L^p},~~~2<p\leq \frac{A_R+B_R+2}{A_R+1},
\end{equation*}
where $\delta=\frac{1}{B_R+1}\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)$.\\

label: lemma-frac-integral-oper
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to consider the case $b=\frac12$. Without loss of generality, assume $f$ is a positive function in $L^2(0,1)$. Then
\begin{eqnarray*}
\int_0^1|Tf(x)|^2dx
&=&
\int_0^1
\left(
\int_0^1\int_0^1
|x-y_1^a|^{-\frac12}
|x-y_2^a|^{-\frac12}
f(y_1)f(y_2)dy_1dy_2
\right)dx\\
&=&
\int_0^1\int_0^1
\left(
\int_0^1
|x-y_1^a|^{-\frac12}
|x-y_2^a|^{-\frac12}dx
\right)f(y_1)f(y_2)dy_1dy_2.
\end{eqnarray*}
For $u,v\in [-1,1]$, it is easy to see that
\begin{equation*}
\int_{-1}^1|x-u|^{-\frac12}|x-v|^{-\frac12}dx
\leq
C\log\left(\frac{4}{|u-v|}\right)
\end{equation*}
with $C$ independent of $u,v$. By dividing the integral into two parts, $|x-u|\leq 2|u-v|$ and $2|u-v|\leq |x-u| \leq 4$, one can prove the above inequality. By this inequality, we obtain
\begin{eqnarray*}
\int_0^1|Tf(x)|^2dx
&\lesssim&
\int_0^1\int_0^1
\log\left(\frac{4}{|y_1^a-y_2^a|}\right)
f(y_1)f(y_2)dy_1dy_2\\
&\lesssim&
\int_0^1\int_0^1
|y_1^a-y_2^a|^{-\epsilon}
f(y_1)f(y_2)dy_1dy_2
\end{eqnarray*}
for any $\epsilon>0$. Choose $0<\epsilon<\,{\rm min}\{\frac{1}{2a},\frac12\}$. By changes of variables, $u=y_1^a$ and $v=y_2^a$,
\begin{equation*}
\int_0^1\int_0^1
|y_1^a-y_2^a|^{-2\epsilon}dy_1dy_2
=
\frac{1}{a^2}\int_0^1\int_0^1
|u-v|^{-2\epsilon}u^{\frac1a-1}v^{\frac1a-1}dudv
<\infty.
\end{equation*}
By Cauchy-Schwarz's inequality, one gets $\|Tf\|_{L^2(0,1)}\lesssim \|f\|_{L^2(0,1)}$.

If all coefficients $a_n$ are not real numbers, then $|x-r(y)|\geq |x-|a_1|y^{\delta}|$ and the $L^2$ boundedness of $\widetilde{T}$ follows immediately. Assume $\,{\rm Re}\,(r(y))\neq 0$. It is clear that $|x-r(y)|\geq |x-\,{\rm Re}\,(r(y))|$. Without loss of generality, we assume all $a_n$ are real. By a change of variables, our desired result is a consequence of the $L^2$ boundedness for $T$. The proof of the lemma is complete.

title: \bf Definition
body_md: Let $n$ be a positive integer. A series $s(x)$ is said to be a convergent Puiseux series if $s(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_kx^{k/n}$ and the power series $s(x^n)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_kx^{k}$ has a positive convergence radius. For each $\omega$ with $\omega^n=1$, the series $s_\omega(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k\omega^k x^{k/n}$ is said to be a conjugate series to $s(x)$.

label: Def-semi-trans-inva
title: \bf Definition
body_md:
\label{Def-semi-trans-inva}
Assume $S$ is a real analytic function in a neighborhood of the origin in $\mathbb{R}^2$. If its Hessian $S_{xy}''$ can be written as $$S_{xy}''(x,y)=U(x,y)\prod_{i=1}^{N}(x-r_{i}(y))$$ with $N\geq 1$, where $U(0,0)\neq 0$ and $r_1,\cdots,r_N$ are convergent Puiseux series, $r_i(0)=0$, and $r_i'(0)=1$ for all $i=1,2,\cdots,N$. Then $S$ is said to be an almost translation invariant function.

title: \bf Definition
body_md:
A submanifold $M \subseteq \Bbb R^n$ with positive codimension is invariant under $\gamma$ to infinite order at $0 \in \Bbb R^n$ if, for all $(x,t)$ in a small neighborhood of $(0,0)\in M \times \Bbb R^k$,
$$ \text{dist}\left( \gamma(x,t), M \right)=O\left( (|x|+|t|)^N \right),\ (x,t)\rightarrow (0,0)\in \Bbb R^n \times \Bbb R^k $$
for any $N\geq 1$.

If there exists no submanifold $M \subseteq \Bbb R^n$, with positive codimension, such that $M$ is invariant under $\gamma$ to infinite order at $0 \in \Bbb R^n$, then $\gamma$ is said to satisfy curvature condition $\mathcal{C}_M$.
head: environment

title: {\bf Remark}
body_md: If the mapping $\gamma_t(x)$ is real-analytic with respect to $x$ and $t$, then the curvature condition $\mathcal{C}_M$ can be defined by the notion of invariant submanifold; see \cite{Christ-Nagel-Stein-Wainger}.
head: environment

title: \bf Definition
body_md:
For $(x,t)$ in a small neighborhood of $(0,0)\in \Bbb R^n \times \Bbb R^k$, consider the 2n-fold iteration
$$\Gamma(x;t_1,t_2,\dots,t_{2n-1},t_{2n})
=\gamma_{t_{2n}}\circ \gamma_{t_{2n-1}}\circ \dots \gamma_{t_2}\circ \gamma_{t_1}(x)$$
with $\tau=(t_1,t_2,\dots,t_{2n-1},t_{2n})\in \Bbb R^{2nk}$. If there exist $n$ coordinates $\xi_1,\xi_2,\dots,\xi_n$ of $\tau$ and a multiindex $\alpha \in \Bbb N^{2nk}$ such that
$$ \partial_{\tau}^\alpha J(x,\xi)\neq 0, ~~~J(x,\xi)=\det\left(\frac{\partial \Gamma(x,\tau)}{\partial (\xi_1,\dots,\xi_n)}\right)$$
for all $(x,\tau)$ near $(0,0)\in \Bbb R^n\times \Bbb R^{2nk}$, then $\gamma_t(x)$ satisfies curvature condition $\mathcal{C}_J$.
head: environment

title: \bf Definition
body_md: Assume $\gamma (x,t)$, satisfying $\gamma(x,0)\equiv x$, is a smooth mapping from $V \subseteq \Bbb R^n \times \Bbb R^k$ into $\Bbb R^n$, where $V$ is a neighborhood of the origin in $\Bbb R^n \times \Bbb R^k$. If the collection of vector fields $\{X_\alpha :\alpha \in \Bbb N^k\}$ satisfies that $X_\alpha,\alpha \in \Bbb N^k$, together with all their commutators span $\Bbb R^n$ at $0\in \Bbb R^n$, then $\gamma$ satisfies curvature condition $\mathcal{C}_\mathfrak{g}$.
head: environment

label: Christ's theorem
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{Christ's theorem}
Assume $T$ is the singular Radon transform defined by {\rm(\ref{Singular-RT})}. If $\gamma_t$ satisfies one of the three curvature conditions $\mathcal{C}_M$, $\mathcal{C}_J$, and $\mathcal{C}_\mathfrak{g}$, then $T$ is bounded from $L^p(\Bbb R^n)$ into itself for every $1<p<\infty$.
head: environment

label: Thm-Maximal-RT
title: \bf Theorem
head: environment

label: Def-Tj
title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a $C_0^\infty$ function $\eta$, $supp(\eta)\subseteq\{t\in \Bbb R^k:a/2\leq |t|\leq 2a\}$, such that $\sum_{j\in \Bbb Z}\eta (t/2^j)=1$ for $t\neq 0$. For $j\geq 0$,
\begin{equation}\label{Def-Tj}
T_jf(x)=\psi(x)\int_{\Bbb R^k}f(\gamma_t(x))K(t)\eta (2^jt)dt.
\end{equation}
Write $K_j(t)=K(t)\eta(2^jt), j\geq 0, j\in \Bbb N.$ Let the maximal operator $T^\ast$ be defined by
$$T^\ast f(x)=\sup_{m\geq 0}\left|\sum_{j=0}^m T_j f(x)\right|.$$
We are going to prove that $T^\ast$ is bounded from $L^p(\Bbb R^n)$ into itself for $1<p<\infty$.

For each $m>0$, decompose
\begin{equation}\label{decomposition}
\sum_{j=0}^m T_jf(x)=S_m\left(\sum_{j=0}^m T_jf\right)(x)+\left(I-S_m\right)\sum_{j=0}^mT_jf(x),
\end{equation}
where $I$ is the identity operator. For the first term,
$$S_m\left(\sum_{j=0}^m T_j f\right)=S_m Tf-S_m\left(\sum_{j=m+1}^\infty T_j f\right).$$
Then $S_m(Tf)$ is majorized by a constant multiple of $M(Tf)$, where the maximal operator $M$ is defined with repsect to the quasi-metric $d$. On the other hand, $S_m\left(\sum_{j=m+1}^\infty T_jf\right)$ is also bounded by $O(Mf(x))$, with the implicit constant independent of $m$. To see this,
observe that
\begin{eqnarray*}
&&
S_m\left(\sum_{j=m+1}^\infty T_j\right)f(x)\nonumber\\
&=&\sum_{j=m+1}^\infty \int_{\Bbb R^n} S_m(x,y)\left(\int_{\Bbb R^k}\psi(y)f(\gamma_t(y))K(t)\eta (2^jt)dt\right)dy\nonumber\\
&=&\sum_{j=m+1}^\infty \int_{\Bbb R^n}S_m(x,\gamma_t^{-1}(y)) \left(\int_{\Bbb R^k}\psi(\gamma_t^{-1}(y))f(y)K(t)\eta (2^j t)\det\left(\frac{\partial \gamma_t^{-1}(y)}{\partial y}\right) dt\right)dy.\nonumber
        \end{eqnarray*}
For each $j$, $j\geq m+1$, one has
\begin{eqnarray*}
S_m(x,\gamma_t^{-1}(y)&=&
S_m(x,y)+
 O\left(2^{m(Q+\frac{1}{N})}|t|^{1/N}\right),\\
 \psi(\gamma_t^{-1}(y))&=&\psi(y)+O(|t|),\\
 \det\left(\frac{\partial \gamma_t^{-1}(y)}{\partial y}\right)&=&1+O(|t|).
 \end{eqnarray*}
Using these estimates, we can see that
$$\sup_{m\geq 0}\left|
S_m\left(\sum_{j=m+1}^{\infty}T_j\right)f(x)
 \right|\lesssim Mf(x).$$
Now we turn to the second term in (\ref{decomposition}). Observe that $$(I-S_m)\sum_{j=0}^mT_j
=\sum_{j=-\infty}^0(I-S_m)T_{j+m}.$$
Here $T_k=0$ for $k<0$, by the definition of $T_j$ in (\ref{Def-Tj}). It suffices to show that for every $1<p<\infty,$
$$\left\| \left(\sum_{m=0}^\infty |(I-S_m)T_{j+m}f|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \right\|_{L^p(\Bbb R^n)}\leq C 2^{\epsilon j}\Vert f\Vert_{L^p(\Bbb R^n)},$$
where $C$ and $\epsilon >0$ are independent of $j\leq 0$. Let $\gamma_m(t)$ be the Rademacher functions on $[0,1]$. Then the above inequality can be deduced by
\begin{equation}\label{Esti-ell2-squre-function}
\left\| \sum_{m=0}^\infty \gamma_m(t)(I-S_m)T_{j+m}
f\right\|_{L^p(\Bbb R^n)}\leq C2^{\epsilon j}
\| f\|_{L^p(\Bbb R^n)}
\end{equation}
for $C$ and $\epsilon>0$ independent of $j$ and $t\in [0,1]$.

For every $1<p<\infty$, taking the adjoint operator, we reduce (\ref{Esti-ell2-squre-function}) to
$$\left\| \sum_{m=0}^\infty \gamma_m(t)T_{j+m}^\ast(I-S_m)\right\|_{L^{p'}\rightarrow L^{p'}}\leq C 2^{\epsilon j},~~~p'=\frac{p}{p-1}.$$
Here we make use of $S_m^\ast=S_m$. Since $p'$ can take any value in $(1,\infty)$, it suffices to show
$$\left\| \sum_{m=0}^\infty \gamma_m(t)T_{j+m}^\ast(I-S_m)\right\|_{L^{p}\rightarrow L^{p}}\leq C 2^{\epsilon j},~~~1<p<\infty$$
with $\epsilon>0$ depending on $p$. In view of
$$T_{j+m}^\ast=T_{j+m}'+E_{j+m},$$
with $\Vert E_{j+m}\Vert_{p\rightarrow p}=O(2^{-(j+m)})$, it suffices to show
$$\left\| \sum_{m=0}^\infty \gamma_m(t)T_{j+m}'(I-S_m)\right\|_{L^p\rightarrow L^p}\leq C2^{\epsilon j}.$$
Write $T_{j+m}'$ by $\widetilde{T}_{j+m}$. Then
\begin{eqnarray*}
\sum\limits_{m=0}^\infty \gamma_m(t)\widetilde{T}_{j+m}(I-S_m)f(x)
 &=& \sum\limits_{m=0}^\infty \gamma_m(t) \widetilde{T}_{j+m}
 \left(\sum\limits_{v=0}^{\infty}R_{m+v}\right)
 f(x)\nonumber\\
 &=& \sum\limits_{v=0}^{\infty} \left(\sum\limits_{m=0}^\infty \gamma_m(t)\widetilde{T}_{j+m}R_{m+v}f\right)
 \nonumber\\
 &=& \sum\limits_{v=0}^\infty \left(\sum\limits_{m=0}^\infty \gamma_{m-j}(t)\widetilde{T}_m R_{m+v-j }f\right).\nonumber
 \end{eqnarray*}
By the estimates (16.3) and (16.4) in \cite{Christ-Nagel-Stein-Wainger}, we have
$$\left\| \sum_{m=0}^\infty \gamma_{m-j}(t)\widetilde{T}_m R_{m+v-j}\right\|_{L^2\rightarrow L^2}\leq C2^{-\epsilon(v-j)}$$
for some $\epsilon >0$, and
$$\left\| \sum_{m=0}^\infty \gamma_{m-j}(t)\widetilde{T}_m
 R_{m+v-j}\right\|_{L^p\rightarrow L^p}\leq C_{p,\epsilon'}2^{\epsilon'(v-j)}$$
for some $\epsilon'>0$ and $1<p\leq 2$.
By interpolation, we obtain for $1<p\leq 2$,
\begin{equation}\label{(6)}
\left\| \sum_{m=0}^\infty \gamma_{m-j}(t)
\widetilde{T}_mR_{m+j-v}\right\|_{L^p\rightarrow L^p}\leq C2^{-\epsilon(v-j)}
\end{equation}
for some $\epsilon>0$, where $C$ is independent of $t\in [0,1]$. By a simple duality argument, we see that (\ref{(6)}) is also true for $2<p<\infty$. This completes the proof of the theorem.

title: {\bf Remark}
body_md:
The operators $T_j^\ast$ and $\widetilde{T}_j$ are given by
$$T_j^\ast f(x)=\int_{|t|\leq a}f(\gamma_t^{-1}(x))
\overline{\gamma}_t^{-1}(x)\overline{K}_j(t)
\det\left(\frac{\partial \gamma_t^{-1}(x)}{\partial x}\right)dt,$$

$$\widetilde{T}_jf(x)= \overline{\psi}(x)\int_{|t|\leq a} f(\gamma_t^{-1}(x))\overline{K}_j(t)dt.$$

label: S6lemma1
title: \bf Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $M=\{(x_1(\tau),x_2(\tau)):\tau \in (-\epsilon_0,\epsilon_0)\}$ is an invariant submanifold for $\gamma_t(x)$ at $(0,0)\in \mathbb{R}^2\times \mathbb{R}$, where $\epsilon_0>0$ is a small number, and $x_1(\tau), x_2(\tau)$ are smooth satisfying $x_1(0)=x_2(0)=0$ and $(x_1',x_2')\neq (0,0)$. Then
$$\left(x_1(\tau)-t,x_2(\tau)-S\left(x_1(\tau),x_1(\tau)-t\right)\right)\in M$$
for all small $\tau,t\in \mathbb{R}$. Let $\tau =0$. Then $\left(-t,-S(0,-t)\right)\in M$ for all small $t$. It follows immediately that $(\tau,-S(0,\tau))\in M$ for small $\tau \in \mathbb{R}$. Hence it is true that
$$(\tau-t,-S(0,\tau)-S(\tau,\tau-t))\in M$$
for every small $\tau,t\in \mathbb{R}$. This implies $S(0,\tau-t)=S(0,\tau)+S(\tau,\tau-t)$. By a change of variables, $u=\tau,v =\tau-t$, we obtain
$$S(u,v)=S(0,v)-S(0,u)$$
for small $u,v$. It is easy to see that the Hessian $S''_{uv}$ vanishes identically. This contradicts our assumption (\ref{Sxy}). The proof of the lemma is complete.
head: environment

label: S6lemma2
title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{S6lemma2}
Assume $\gamma_t(x)=\left(x_1-t,x_2-S(x_1,x_1-t)\right)$ is the same as in (\ref{S6lemma1}). Then $\gamma_t$ satisfies the curvature condition $\mathcal{C}_J$.

title: \bf Lemma
body_md:
\label{S6lemma3}
Assume $\gamma_t(x)=(x_1-t,x_2-S(x_1,x_1-t))$ with $S$ having Hessian of the form (\ref{Sxy}). Then $\gamma_t$ satisfies the curvature condition $\mathcal{C}_\mathfrak{g}$.
head: environment

label: exponential-expansion
title: Proof
body_md:
For smooth functions $f$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$,
$$
\frac{d}{dt}(f(\gamma_t(x)))
=
-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(\gamma_t(x))
+
\frac{\partial S}{\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1-t)\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(\gamma_t(x)).$$
Let $X(t)=-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}+\frac{\partial S}{\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1-t)\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}.$ Then
\begin{eqnarray*}
X(t)^2
&=&
\left(-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}+\frac{\partial S}{\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1-t)\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}\right)^2\\
&=&
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_1^2}
-2\frac{\partial S}{\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1-t)
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}
+
\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1-t) \right)^2 \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_2^2}\\
& &
-\frac{\partial^2S}{\partial x_1 \partial x_2}(x_1,x_1-t)\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}
-
\frac{\partial^2S}{\partial x_2^2}(x_1,x_1-t)
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}.
\end{eqnarray*}
With this equality, we obtain
\begin{eqnarray*}
\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\left(f(\gamma_t(x))\right)
&=&
\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_1^2}(\gamma_t(x))
-2\frac{\partial S}{\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1-t)
\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}(\gamma_t(x))\\
& &
+
\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1-t) \right)^2 \frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_2^2}(\gamma_t(x))
-\frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial x_2^2}(x_1,x_1-t)
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(\gamma_t(x))\\
&=&
(X^2(t)f)(\gamma_t(x))
+
\frac{\partial^2S}{\partial x_1 \partial x_2}(x_1,x_1-t)\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(\gamma_t(x)).
\end{eqnarray*}
In view of (\ref{exponential-of-gamma}), there are smooth vector fields $X_k$, defined near the origin of $\mathbb{R}^2$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{exponential-expansion}
\gamma_t(x)\sim \exp\left(\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{t^k}{k!}X_k\right)(x),~~~ t\rightarrow 0.
\end{equation}
Hence we also have
$$f(\gamma_t(x))
=
f(x)+(X_1f)(x)t+\frac{1}{2!}(X_2f+X_1^2f)(x)t^2+O(t^3),
~~~ t\rightarrow 0.$$
Hence we obtain $$X_1=X(0)=\left(-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}+\frac{\partial S}{\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}\right)|_x.$$
By direct calculation, it is easy to see that
$$X_2=\frac{\partial^2S}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}|_x.$$
Since $\frac{\partial^2S}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}$ is a real-analytic function near the origin, we can divide our argument into two cases, depending on whether $\frac{\partial^2S}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)$ vanishes identically.

If $\frac{\partial^2S}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)$ is not identical to zero, then for some $k\in \mathbb{N}$ and small $x_1$,  $$\frac{d^k}{dx_1^k}\left(\frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)\right)=\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}+\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}\right)^k\frac{\partial^2S}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)\neq 0.$$
We see that $X_1$ and $(ad X_1)^k(X_2)=
\left[X_1,\left[X_1,\left[\cdots,\left[X_1,
X_2\right]\cdots\right]\right]\right]$, with $k$ copies of $X_1$, span the tangent space $\mathbb{R}^2$. Hence $\gamma_t$ satisfies the condition $\mathcal{C}_\mathfrak{g}$.

Now consider the case $\frac{\partial^2S}{\partial x_1\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)\equiv 0$ for small $x_1$. Let $M\geq 0$ be the smallest integer such that
\begin{equation}\label{vanishing-condition}
\frac{\partial^{l+2}S}{\partial x_1^{l+1}\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)\equiv 0~~~\textrm{for~~$0\leq l \leq M$}.
\end{equation}
By the factorization (\ref{Sxy}), our assumption on $S$ implies that $0\leq M \leq N-1$. For integers $p,q\geq 0$ and $p+q\leq M$, we also have
 \begin{equation*}
\frac{\partial^{p+q+2}S}{\partial x_1^{p+1}\partial x_2^{q+1}}(x_1,x_1)\equiv 0.
\end{equation*}
For two arbitrary constants $C_1,C_2$, let $f(x)=C_1x_1+C_2x_2$. For $m\geq 2$, one can verify easily that
\begin{equation*}
\frac{d^m}{dt^m}\Big( f(\gamma_t(x) )\Big)
=
C_2(-1)^{m-1}\frac{\partial^m S}{\partial x_2^m}
(x_1,x_1-t).
\end{equation*}
By an induction argument, one has $X_k=0$ for $2\leq k \leq M+2$, where the vector fields $X_k$ are given by (\ref{exponential-expansion}). Then $X_{M+3}$ satisfies
$$X_{M+3}f+X_1^{M+3}f=C_2(-1)^{M+2}
\frac{\partial^{M+3} S}{\partial x_2^{M+3}}
(x_1,x_1).$$
Observe that $f(x)=C_1x_1+C_2x_2$. Hence, using (\ref{vanishing-condition}),
\begin{eqnarray*}
X_1^{M+3}f(x)
&= &
C_2(-1)^{M+2}\frac{d^{M+2}}{d x_1^{M+2}}
\Big( \frac{\partial S}{\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)\Big)\\
&= &
C_2(-1)^{M+2}\frac{\partial^{M+3} S}{\partial x_1^{M+2}\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)
+
C_2(-1)^{M+2}\frac{\partial^{M+3} S}{\partial x_2^{M+3}}(x_1,x_1).
\end{eqnarray*}
This gives
\begin{equation*}
X_{M+3}=(-1)^{M+3}\frac{\partial^{M+3} S}{\partial x_1^{M+2}\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}.
\end{equation*}
By our definition of $M$, the function $\frac{\partial^{M+3}S}{\partial x_1^{M+2}\partial x_2}(x_1,x_1)$ does not vanish identically near the origin. There exists a nonnegative integer $k$ such that $X_1$ and $(adX_1)^{k}(X_{M+3})$ span the full tangent space $\mathbb{R}^2$. This proves that $\gamma_t$ satisfies the condition $\mathcal{C}_\mathfrak{g}$. Hence our proof is complete.

label: Thm-Regularity-Unbouned-Faces
title: \bf Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm-Regularity-Unbouned-Faces}
Assume $S$ is a real-valued real analytic function near the origin in the plane. Let the Radon transform $Rf$ be defined as in {\rm(1.1)}, $(A_L,B_L)$ the leftmost extreme point of $N(S_{xy}'')$. Then the following statements are true.
\vspace{0.5\baselineskip}

\noindent {\rm(i)} If $A_L\geq B_L$, then there exits a constant $C>0$ such that
$$\|Rf\|_{L_{\delta}^p(\mathbb{R}^2)}\leq C\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^2)},~~~\delta=\frac{1}{(A_L+1)p},
~~~2\leq p \leq \infty.$$
\noindent{\rm(ii)} If $A_L<B_L$, then
$$\|Rf\|_{L_\delta^p(\mathbb{R}^2)}\leq C\|f\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^2)},~~~ \delta=\frac{1}{(A_L+1)p},$$
where $\frac{A_L+B_L+2}{A_L+1}<p\leq +\infty$.
head: environment

title: {\bf Remark}
body_md: As shown in $\S$3, the statement in (i) is not true for all $\frac{A_L+B_L+2}{A_L+1}\leq p <2$. In other words, if $A_L>B_L$ then the critical Sobolev regularity breaks down on a bounded segment of the left unbounded face of $N_r(S)$.
